analysis.one_liner: Bars states from setting their own food safety warnings and labeling rules stricter than federal standards.
analysis.headline: The Senate Agriculture Committee reported the bill in October 2000, but it never got a Senate floor vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal food law to prohibit states and localities from enforcing any food safety warning, notification, or labeling requirement that is not identical to federal rules. States could keep only a list of specific rules like open-date labeling, organic designations, unit pricing, and geographic origin. A state could apply for a federal exemption for a unique rule, or act unilaterally only in a narrow 'imminent hazard' emergency, and would otherwise have to rely on federal agencies to set any new protections.
analysis.who_benefits: Food manufacturers and distributors, who would deal with one set of national warning and labeling rules instead of a patchwork of stricter state requirements; also grocery chains and brand-name product makers who would no longer face state-mandated warning labels on products sold nationally.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any state or local government from establishing or keeping a food safety warning or notification requirement that is not identical to federal law, covering disclosures on labels, posters, advertising, and other communications by manufacturers and distributors [S3] [S4].
Extends the same uniformity mandate to dietary supplement labeling and to state food adulteration requirements, wiping out stricter state standards that differ from federal ones [S3].

Lets states petition the federal health secretary for an exemption for a state rule that protects an important public interest, or to seek a national standard, but places the decision with federal regulators rather than the state [S3] [S4].

Allows states to keep specific listed rules such as freshness dating, open-date labeling, grade labeling, religious dietary labeling, organic or natural designations, returnable bottle labeling, unit pricing, geographic origin, and certain food sanitation advisories [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and state health officials, who would lose the ability to require warnings stricter than federal ones on foods and dietary supplements, and states generally, which would surrender much of their traditional police power over food safety to federal regulators and the federal petition process.

drawbacks.text: States and localities could no longer set warning or notification requirements stricter than federal law, even where federal rules do not exist or are weaker, eliminating a major source of state food safety protections for consumers [S3] [S4].

States could not unilaterally protect residents except by proving an 'imminent hazard' likely to cause serious health consequences or death, a high emergency bar, and would otherwise have to rely on a federal petition process with strict deadlines and judicial review [S4].

Even a long-standing state rule would be wiped out 180 days after enactment unless the state successfully petitioned for an exemption, meaning existing consumer warnings would be lost by default if a state did not or could not act in time [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Uniform national rules would simplify compliance for food companies and might lower some costs, but the bill would do so by shifting food safety authority from states to federal regulators and by default eliminating stricter state warnings, including for dietary supplements, unless states win exemptions through a federal petition process. The public's main protections under state law — state-specific safety warnings — would be removed, and states' room to respond to new hazards would be sharply limited.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Agriculture Committee approved and reported the bill to the full Senate in October 2000, but no vote ever happened on the Senate floor before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Introduced in the Senate in May 1999 and referred to the Agriculture Committee [S6].
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in June 2000 and formally reported it in October 2000, placing it on the Senate calendar of business [S6].
Despite being placed on the calendar, the bill never received a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 [S1] [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments and consumer protection authority were left intact, since no stricter federal preemption was enacted; food manufacturers did not get the national uniformity they sought.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start, with 26 Republican and 10 Democratic Senate cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would replace a patchwork of stricter state warning and labeling rules with a single federal standard, reducing compliance costs but also removing state-level warnings consumers could otherwise rely on.
State dietary supplement labeling rules not identical to federal law would be barred, a notable loss of state oversight in an industry with historically limited federal regulation.
States would lose much of their authority to set their own food safety and labeling standards, a traditional exercise of state police power.
